analysis:
The only change is in the test helper provider-swift/Tests/ProviderCoreTests/Helpers/MockCoordinator.swift, in dropActiveWebSocket (head lines 445-458). It now takes a configurable close code (default 1001) and an optional reason, so tests can inject a 1012 close like the one the edge sends on a Conductor change. It replaces the fixed .goingAway / "mock dropping" close. The default behavior is the same as before, apart from the reason now being an optional parameter.

Security relevance: this is test-only code. It binds to 127.0.0.1:0, runs only in the test target, and does not ship in the provider binary. It adds no production attack surface and touches none of the assets or boundaries. Specifically it does not touch the TB-002 provider/coordinator contract, the T-041 cache, the attestation chain, or App Attest. `.init(codeNumber: Int(closeCode))` converts a UInt16, so there is no overflow. The mock does not validate signatures and says so (lines 14-17). Its retired /v1/telemetry/events route captures any POST as a privacy-regression trap, which supports the threat model's no-telemetry posture. The mock handles every ProviderMessage case, including App Attest and capacity messages.

Open question for later passes: how the provider's reconnect loop handles a 1012 close, in production source outside this batch. That could matter for availability and for T-053 (stale authorization after a connection change). Nothing in the supplied evidence shows a regression there.
